## Statement
```cpp
int longest_even_vowels(const std::string& s);
    // longest substring in which each of a, e, i, o, u occurs an EVEN number of times (0 counts as even)
long long count_wonderful(const std::string& s);
    // substrings (letters a–j only) in which AT MOST ONE letter occurs an odd number of times
```

**Parity masks.** Keep a bitmask where bit `v` is the parity (even = 0, odd = 1) of letter `v`'s count in the prefix so far. A substring's parities are the XOR of the masks at its two ends.

- **Even vowels:** the masks at the two ends must be **equal**. Store the first index of each mask (32 possible masks for 5 vowels).
- **At most one odd:** the two masks are equal, or they differ in exactly **one** bit. Count the earlier masks equal to the current mask, plus each of the 10 one-bit flips (1024 possible masks for letters a–j).

**Input:** lines `even s` or `wonder s` until the end of input (|s| ≤ 10⁶).

## Starter
```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int longest_even_vowels(const string& s) { return 0; }
long long count_wonderful(const string& s) { return (long long)s.size(); }
```

## Driver
```cpp
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    string cmd, s;
    while (cin >> cmd >> s) {
        if (cmd == "even") cout << longest_even_vowels(s) << '\n';
        else cout << count_wonderful(s) << '\n';
    }
}
```

## Hints
- You only need to know whether each vowel's count is even or odd, and five such bits form a mask.
- The substring between two equal prefix masks has all-even counts. Store the first index of each mask (seed the empty prefix at −1).
- For "at most one odd", also count the earlier masks that differ from the current one in exactly one bit.

## Solution
**Parity is all that matters.** "Even count in the substring" means the prefix counts at the two ends have the same parity. Packing five (or ten) parities into a bitmask turns the condition into "the masks are equal". That's the prefix-XOR trick with a hashable state.

There are only 32 (or 1024) masks, so a plain array is the hash table.

**Longest:** for equal masks, the earliest occurrence gives the longest substring ending here.

**Counting "at most one odd":** the end masks must be equal (zero odd letters) or differ in exactly one bit (one odd letter). For each prefix, add the counts of the current mask and of its 10 single-bit neighbours.

The results reach about n²/2, so use `long long`.

Complexity: O(n) and O(10·n).

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int longest_even_vowels(const string& s) {
    array<int, 32> first;
    first.fill(INT_MAX);
    first[0] = -1;                                       // empty prefix
    int mask = 0, best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)s.size(); ++i) {
        switch (s[i]) {
            case 'a': mask ^= 1; break;  case 'e': mask ^= 2; break;
            case 'i': mask ^= 4; break;  case 'o': mask ^= 8; break;
            case 'u': mask ^= 16; break; default: break;
        }
        if (first[mask] == INT_MAX) first[mask] = i;     // first time we see this parity state
        else best = max(best, i - first[mask]);          // equal masks => all-even substring
    }
    return best;
}

long long count_wonderful(const string& s) {
    array<long long, 1024> cnt{};
    cnt[0] = 1;
    int mask = 0; long long res = 0;
    for (char c : s) {
        mask ^= 1 << (c - 'a');
        res += cnt[mask];                                // all letters even
        for (int b = 0; b < 10; ++b) res += cnt[mask ^ (1 << b)];   // exactly one letter odd
        ++cnt[mask];
    }
    return res;
}
```
